newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Afghans turn swords to ploughshares.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Afghans turn swords to ploughshares.

text.p: After seventeen years of war, Afghanistan is awash with weapons and the debris of battle, but in a corner of the capital Kabul some of them are being put to constructive use.
Like the biblical image of swords into ploughshares, tanks and rockets are being turned into agricultural implements.
In a workshop the size of the average lock-up garage Enayatullah is turning plate metal from destroyed tanks into shovels, pick axes and hoes.
"We buy armour plating from people in the market who dismantle tanks that have been destroyed in the war." says Enayatullah. "Then we make tools out of it."
The operation is entirely manual. In the darkened workshop Enayatullah and his two sons and a grandson beat out a tattoo with sledge hammers as they thin the glowing pieces of armour plate.
A young boy, the whites of his eyes a stark contrast to his blackened face, monotonously turns the handle of an air pump that heats the forge.

Part of Enayatullah's work is supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). In return for food, he supplies shovels to the ICRC which they then give to impoverished farmers and refugees returning to their land.
Enayatullah is contracted to produce 10 shovels per day for the ICRC.
Afghanistan's population is 85 percent rural, and the agricultural sector has been devastated by the war.

Much of the fighting occured in the country's most fertile regions. Fields were sown with mines, irrigation ditches were bombed or allowed to silt up, and whole villages fled to the refugee camps of Pakistan and Iran.
In all, almost a third of the population left the country during the war against the communists.
The ICRC, the United Nations and other organisations are trying to help Afghanistan's farmers rebuild their livelihoods.
De-mining agencies have cleared some of the most productive land, the UN and the ICRC are running food-for-work programmes to clear the irrigation systems.
But once the land has been cleared, the farmers need tools to farm it.
Mir Aqa Noori, who is in charge of the Red Cross's tools for peace programme, says it fulfills two needs.
"It is much cheaper to produce the tools here." said Noori. "A pair of pruning shears that would cost $16 to import from outside can be made for $1 here."
"It also takes some of the weapons out of the war." says Noori.
Hamayoun, aged 20, used to man a guard post behind his house until he started on the tools for peace programme.

Now he buys rocket propelled grenades from which the explosive has been removed and melts down the aluminium to make handles for the shears. Then he grinds blades from forged steel scavenged from disabled Soviet-built armoured vehicles before fitting the shears with a spring taken from a Kalashnikov assault rifle.
The ICRC's Noori says that at least 200 otherwise lethal rocket-propelled grenades have been metamorphosed into useful tools.
There is no shortage of raw materials. Afghanistan is littered with detritus from the war. Along the main corridors of battle lie the rusting hulks of tanks and armored vehicles.
In the absence of any large-scale industry, recycling war debris has become one of the major sources of income for Afghans.
